readerTitle: The $300 bonus that made a restaurant worse
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당, 상업 청소 회사, 소프트웨어 회사 고객지원팀) · 모든 상황과 금액은 설명용
insight: 보너스를 설계할 때는 금액보다 두 가지를 먼저 묻는다. 사람들이 이 숫자를 쫓다가 무엇을 망가뜨릴지, 그리고 옆 사람과 비교했을 때 공정하게 느껴질지.
misconception: 가장 잘한 직원 한 명에게 큰 보너스를 주면 모두가 더 열심히 일한다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 PPL-04-06 (When incentives backfire), PPL-04-03 (Fairness)
모든 사례와 금액은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례와 금액($300 보너스 등)은 가상입니다. 실제 연구나 기업 수치는 사용하지 않았습니다.
팁 공유(tip pooling)와 보너스 지급 방식은 나라와 지역마다 법 규정이 다릅니다. 레슨은 팁이 아닌 업주가 주는 보너스만 다루며 법률 조언을 하지 않습니다. 게시 전 문구에 팁과 혼동될 표현이 없는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The $300 bonus that made a restaurant worse
body: Dana owns a busy neighborhood restaurant. Sales are flat, so she announces a bonus: **$300 each month** to the server with the highest average bill per table.
Four weeks later, average bills are up. So are complaints. Regulars say they feel pushed, and the kitchen has stopped talking to the floor staff.

image.label: A server pushing a dessert menu at a tired-looking table
image.brief: 따뜻한 조명의 동네 식당. 서버가 과하게 웃으며 디저트 메뉴를 내밀고, 손님은 시계를 보며 곤란한 표정. 뒤쪽 주방 창 너머로 요리사가 팔짱을 끼고 지켜봄. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: How would you fix Dana's bonus?
body: Dana still wants to lift sales, and she has the same $300 a month to spend. Which redesign would you pick?

options.text: Keep the top-server prize, but raise it to $500 to make it count
options.feedback: A bigger prize sharpens the same problems: more pushing at tables and more resentment from everyone who can't win it. That's an incentive backfiring.

options.text: Share the $300 across floor and kitchen when monthly sales and review scores both hit a target
options.feedback: Pairing sales with reviews blocks the shortcut of pushing guests. Including the kitchen makes the reward feel fair to the people who also made those sales.

options.text: Drop the targets and split $300 equally every month
options.feedback: It feels fair, and nobody games anything. But it stops pointing anyone at a goal, and soon it reads as normal pay.

cards.title: People chase the number, not the goal.
body: Dana wanted happier guests who spend more and come back. She paid for one number: average bill. So servers did what the number rewarded. They upsold hard, nudged guests toward pricey bottles, and fought over the big tables.
This is **when incentives backfire**. A single measure gets hit while the real goal suffers. The fix is to pair the measure with one that catches the shortcut, like return visits or review scores.

cards.title: Everyone who touched the sale is watching.
body: The cooks plated every one of those expensive dishes. The hosts decided who got the big tables. None of them could earn the $300.

**Fairness** is judged by comparison: what I put in and get back, next to what you put in and get back. People also judge the process. Were the rules clear in advance? Could I actually win? When the answer is no, effort drops among exactly the people the business needs.

image.label: One server holding a prize while cooks and hosts look on
image.brief: 한 서버가 큰 리본 봉투를 들고 서 있고, 옆에서 요리사, 호스트, 설거지 담당이 빈손으로 바라봄. 각 인물 위에 작은 말풍선 "I helped too". 밝은 플랫 일러스트, 로고 없음.

cards.title: A bonus can't fix a bad base.
body: If base pay or schedules feel unfair, a bonus on top often reads as a distraction, not a reward.
And once a bonus is paid for a few months, people count on it. Cutting it later feels like a pay cut, even if you called it temporary. Start small, set clear rules, and say up front how long it runs.
cards.softwareNote: The same traps show up with sales commissions and team bonuses in software companies. Paying for signed deals alone can reward deals that churn in three months.

cards.title: Now it's a commercial cleaning company.
body: You run night crews that clean offices for business clients. You want to grow without hiring yet, so you plan a bonus for crews. What should it reward?

options.text: A payment for every extra office a crew cleans per night
options.feedback: You'll get speed, but skipped bins and dusty desks too. The measure rewards the shortcut, a classic backfire, and clients notice before you do.

options.text: A crew-wide bonus based on client renewals and surprise quality checks
options.feedback: Renewals and spot checks catch rushed work, so the measure points at the real goal. Sharing it across the crew keeps it fair to everyone holding a mop.

options.text: A bigger bonus for crew leads only, since they're accountable
options.feedback: Leads may push harder, but the cleaners doing the work get nothing. That gap breeds resentment and quiet effort cuts.

cards.title: Now it's a support team at a software company.
body: You lead customer support. Finance gives you a quarterly bonus budget. Your boss suggests rewarding the agents who close tickets fastest. What do you propose?

options.text: Go with speed: rank agents by average time to close
options.feedback: Agents will close tickets before problems are solved, and reopened tickets will climb. Speed alone is a number that's easy to game.

options.text: A team bonus tied to customer satisfaction and fewer reopened tickets, with rules posted in advance
options.feedback: Two measures check each other, so gaming gets hard. Shared, published rules make the process feel fair, and agents help each other on hard tickets.

options.text: Individual bonuses based on each agent's satisfaction score
options.feedback: Better than speed, but hard tickets earn lower scores. Agents may start dodging them, and whoever gets the tough accounts feels cheated.

cards.title: Ask what people will break, and who is left out.
body: You used two ideas here. **When incentives backfire:** pair any number you pay for with one that catches the shortcut. **Fairness:** include everyone who shapes the result, and publish the rules before the race starts.
**Try it today:** take one bonus or target your business uses. Write down the easiest way to hit it badly, and one person who helps but can't earn it.
